title: The Debate Over Returning Objects
short: Some argue that famous objects taken in colonial times should go back to Egypt; others argue they were acquired legally, are well kept and seen by many. This topic sets out both sides.
trouble: Students expect one obviously right answer. Each case turns on how an object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public.

blocks.html: Some of the best-known objects in museums abroad left Egypt when Egypt was under Ottoman, British or French influence. Egypt has asked for some of them back. Museums holding them have mostly said no. This is a real debate, argued in good faith on both sides; this topic sets out the arguments, not a verdict.

Those who favor return argue that objects taken in colonial times left without fair consent, belong to Egypt's national heritage, and can now be cared for and seen in Egypt's own museums. Those who favor keeping them argue that they were acquired legally under the laws and agreements of the time, have been well kept and studied, and are seen by huge international audiences, and that museums are often barred by law from giving them up. Each case turns on how the object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public.

The debate is hard because the two sides often agree on the facts and disagree on what matters most. A division of finds signed by both parties in 1913 can be legal and still look unfair a century later. A museum in London can serve millions of visitors and still hold an object that many Egyptians see as part of their own story. Reasonable people weigh legality, history, access and care differently.

items: Rosetta Stone. Egypt has asked for its return, or at least a long loan. The British Museum answers that it was acquired under a treaty and that a universal museum serves every nation; in 2005 it gave a full-size replica to Rashid.

Bust of Nefertiti. Egypt has asked for it since the 1920s and argues that the bust's value was concealed in the division. Its German holders answer that the division was signed by both sides and was legal, and that the bust is too fragile to travel.
Dendera zodiac. Egyptians have called for its return to the temple's country. The Louvre has held and shown it for two centuries as part of its collection.

head: For return
For keeping
rows: Removal under colonial power was not a free agreement between equals.
The removal followed the law, treaty or permit of its time; judging it by today's rules is unfair.
These objects are part of Egypt's national identity and history.
They are also part of world heritage, and of the history of the museums that have held them for generations.
Egypt now has world-class museums, such as the Grand Egyptian Museum, able to care for them.
The objects are safe, conserved and studied where they are; moving fragile things carries risk.
Most Egyptians can never travel to London or Berlin to see their own heritage.
Millions of visitors from every country see them in great museums, often free of charge.
Objects belong near their place of origin and context.
Returning one object sets a precedent that could empty museums, and many museums are forbidden by law to give up their collections.

blocks.title: Which side does it support?
blocks.q: "The bust of Nefertiti was allotted to the German team in a division of finds signed by both sides in 1913." Which side does this point support, and what kind of argument is it?
steps: It says the removal followed the agreed rules of the time.
It is a legal argument. The other side answers with a historical one: that the bust's importance was not made clear in the division.

blocks.title: Why one case is different
blocks.q: In 2019 the Metropolitan Museum returned the gilded coffin of Nedjemankh to Egypt, two years after buying it. Why was there no debate in that case?
steps: Investigators showed that the coffin was looted in 2011 and sold with a forged export license.
It was stolen property under the laws in force when it left Egypt, so neither law nor ethics supported keeping it.
The debate over return concerns objects that left legally, or under disputed terms, long ago, not recent thefts.
blocks.a: It was recently stolen, so its case was settled by law, not argued.

blocks.html: Expecting one obviously right answer. Each case turns on how an object was acquired, the laws of the time, and what is best for the object and the public. Before taking a side on any case, find out how that object left Egypt.
Middle paths are also proposed: long-term loans, shared research and exhibitions, replicas and digital access, and returns of objects whose removal was clearly illegal.
